title: HSHD1 Endocrine Practice Question Bank
intended_use: Original educational MCQs written at a second-year-medical-student level. Version 1.0.0 covered hypothalamic-pituitary, thyroid, and diabetes/insulin topics; version 1.1.0 adds the week-2 lectures (Steroid Hormone Synthesis, Adrenal Gland Disorders, and DSD Concepts). The week-2 items were written to the concepts tested by an outside review-question set the student had worked through, then audited against the lecture slides and session objectives so that each one is answerable from the assigned lecture materials alone; items that required outside content were dropped. All stems, options, and explanations are newly authored and are not drawn from or a copy of any commercial or institutional question bank.

schema_notes.option_explanation: Shown after submission for both correct and incorrect selections.
schema_notes.citation: An open-access reference (StatPearls, Endotext, or a professional-society guideline) supporting the concept tested; not a citation to a copied question.

questions.objective: Localize thyroid dysfunction using TSH and free T4
questions.stem: A 14-year-old has fatigue, slowed growth, and constipation. Free T4 is low and TSH is markedly elevated. Which site is most likely responsible for the hormone abnormality?

options.explanation: A hypothalamic defect causes central hypothyroidism, in which TSH is low or inappropriately normal rather than markedly elevated.
Pituitary failure also produces central hypothyroidism with low or inappropriately normal TSH.
Correct. Failure of the thyroid lowers free T4, removing negative feedback and producing a compensatory rise in TSH.
Impaired peripheral conversion can change T3 availability, but it does not produce the classic high-TSH, low-free-T4 pattern of primary hypothyroidism.

questions.takeaway: High TSH plus low free T4 localizes the defect to the thyroid: primary hypothyroidism.

questions.objective: Interpret imaging in congenital hypothyroidism
questions.stem: A newborn has confirmed primary congenital hypothyroidism. A technetium scan shows thyroid tissue at the base of the tongue and no uptake in the usual pretracheal location. Which mechanism best explains this finding?

options.explanation: Dyshormonogenesis impairs synthesis in a present gland; it does not explain thyroid tissue located at the tongue base.
Correct. A lingual thyroid results when thyroid tissue does not complete its normal descent to the anterior neck.
Maternal antibodies can cause transient neonatal hypothyroidism but do not relocate the gland.
TSH deficiency causes central hypothyroidism and would not explain ectopic functioning thyroid tissue.

questions.takeaway: A lingual thyroid is an ectopic gland caused by incomplete embryologic migration.

questions.objective: Relate Graves pathophysiology to diagnostic findings
questions.stem: A patient has tremor, heat intolerance, diffuse goiter, elevated free T4, and suppressed TSH. Radioactive iodine uptake is diffusely increased. Which mechanism best accounts for the findings?

options.text: Destruction of follicles with leakage of stored hormone
options.explanation: Destructive thyroiditis releases stored hormone but suppresses new iodine uptake, producing low uptake.

options.text: An autonomous mutation confined to one thyroid nodule
options.explanation: A single autonomous nodule causes focal rather than diffuse uptake.

options.text: Antibody-mediated stimulation of the TSH receptor
options.explanation: Correct. TSH-receptor-stimulating antibodies activate the entire gland, causing diffuse growth and hormone synthesis.
Exogenous hormone suppresses both TSH and endogenous thyroid activity, so uptake would be low.

questions.takeaway: Diffuse increased uptake indicates whole-gland hormone synthesis, classically from Graves disease.

questions.objective: Distinguish hormone leakage from hormone overproduction
questions.stem: A patient has palpitations, elevated free T4, suppressed TSH, and minimal radioactive iodine uptake throughout the thyroid. Which process best explains this combination?

options.explanation: Diffuse receptor stimulation increases new hormone synthesis and therefore increases iodine uptake.

options.text: Release of preformed hormone from injured follicles
options.explanation: Correct. Follicular injury can release stored hormone while active synthesis and iodine uptake remain suppressed.
A TSH-secreting adenoma produces an elevated or inappropriately normal TSH, not a suppressed TSH.

options.text: Iodine trapping by an autonomous nodule
options.explanation: An autonomous nodule produces a focal area of increased uptake.

questions.takeaway: Thyrotoxicosis with low uptake suggests hormone leakage or an exogenous source, not active glandular overproduction.

questions.objective: Identify medullary carcinoma and MEN2
questions.stem: A patient with a thyroid mass has elevated calcitonin and a germline RET pathogenic variant. Which additional finding would most strongly support MEN2A?

options.explanation: Mucosal neuromas and a marfanoid habitus are characteristic of MEN2B rather than MEN2A.
Correct. MEN2A classically combines medullary thyroid carcinoma, pheochromocytoma, and hyperparathyroidism.
Pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors are associated with MEN1.
Pituitary tumors are part of MEN1, not the defining MEN2A pattern.

questions.takeaway: MEN2A: medullary thyroid carcinoma, pheochromocytoma, and hyperparathyroidism.

questions.objective: Relate pituitary mass effect to visual findings
questions.stem: A pituitary macroadenoma expands superiorly and compresses the central portion of the optic chiasm. Which visual deficit is most likely?

options.explanation: Correct. Compression of crossing nasal retinal fibers causes loss of the temporal visual fields in both eyes.
Monocular blindness results from injury to one optic nerve anterior to the chiasm.
A homonymous deficit localizes posterior to the optic chiasm.
A central scotoma is not the classic visual-field effect of chiasmal compression by a sellar mass.

questions.takeaway: A superiorly expanding sellar mass classically produces bitemporal hemianopsia.

questions.objective: Recognize ischemic anterior pituitary injury
questions.stem: Several months after severe postpartum hemorrhage, a patient reports inability to lactate, fatigue, and amenorrhea. Which pathophysiologic event best explains these findings?

options.explanation: Thyroid failure could cause fatigue but would not unify the loss of lactation and gonadal function after hemorrhage.

options.text: Ischemic necrosis of the enlarged anterior pituitary
options.explanation: Correct. The pituitary enlarges during pregnancy and is vulnerable to hypoperfusion during major obstetric blood loss.

options.text: Hemorrhage into a preexisting adrenal adenoma
options.explanation: An adrenal lesion does not account for loss of prolactin and gonadotropin function.
The presentation reflects multiple anterior pituitary deficiencies, not posterior hormone excess.

questions.takeaway: Postpartum hemorrhage followed by failure to lactate and other pituitary deficits suggests Sheehan syndrome.

questions.objective: Recognize a pituitary emergency
questions.stem: A patient with a known pituitary macroadenoma develops an abrupt severe headache, vomiting, impaired vision, hypotension, and confusion. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.explanation: Empty sella is often incidental or chronic and does not usually cause an abrupt neurologic and hemodynamic collapse.
Correct. Acute hemorrhage or infarction within an adenoma can cause sudden mass effect and acute pituitary failure.
A Rathke cleft cyst is typically a benign, slower-growing cystic lesion.
Isolated GH deficiency does not produce abrupt headache, visual loss, and cardiovascular instability.

questions.takeaway: Sudden headache and visual or hemodynamic deterioration in a patient with a pituitary lesion is apoplexy until proven otherwise.

questions.objective: Explain prolactin elevation from stalk compression
questions.stem: A non-prolactin-secreting suprasellar mass produces a moderate elevation in serum prolactin. Which mechanism is most likely?

options.explanation: Correct. Dopamine normally inhibits lactotrophs; stalk disruption removes that inhibitory signal.
Somatostatin primarily suppresses GH and TSH and does not explain the stalk-effect prolactin rise.
Prolactin receptors act in target tissues; their stimulation does not cause pituitary prolactin secretion.
The kidney does not become the source of prolactin in a patient with stalk compression.

questions.takeaway: Prolactin is tonically inhibited by dopamine, so pituitary-stalk interruption can raise prolactin.

questions.objective: Differentiate central from nephrogenic diabetes insipidus
questions.stem: A patient has polyuria, hypernatremia, high serum osmolality, and very dilute urine. After desmopressin, urine osmolality rises substantially. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.explanation: SIADH causes water retention, hyponatremia, low serum osmolality, and inappropriately concentrated urine.
Primary polydipsia usually lowers serum sodium and osmolality rather than raising them.
Correct. A strong response to desmopressin shows that the kidneys can respond and that the missing signal was AVP.
With nephrogenic AVP resistance, desmopressin produces little or no increase in urine concentration.

questions.takeaway: Desmopressin concentrates urine in central AVP deficiency but has little effect in renal AVP resistance.

questions.objective: Interpret serum and urine findings in SIADH
questions.stem: A patient with small-cell lung carcinoma develops confusion. Sodium is 118 mEq/L, serum osmolality is low, and urine remains concentrated. Which finding is most consistent with the underlying process?

options.explanation: Suppressed aquaporin insertion would reduce water reabsorption and produce dilute urine, as in AVP deficiency.
Correct. Excess AVP maintains water reabsorption and concentrated urine despite hypotonic plasma.
The central disturbance in SIADH is excess free-water retention, not primary sodium retention.

options.text: Failure of the kidney to respond to AVP
options.explanation: AVP resistance produces high-volume dilute urine and tends toward hypernatremia, the opposite pattern.

questions.takeaway: SIADH produces hypotonic hyponatremia with urine that is inappropriately concentrated.

citation.text: StatPearls: Syndrome of Inappropriate Antidiuretic Hormone Secretion

questions.objective: Explain metabolic consequences of absolute insulin deficiency
questions.stem: A child with newly diagnosed T1DM has weight loss despite increased appetite. Which change most directly contributes to the weight loss?

options.text: Increased glucose uptake by skeletal muscle
options.explanation: Insulin deficiency decreases rather than increases insulin-dependent glucose uptake.

options.text: Increased storage of triglyceride in adipose tissue
options.explanation: Insulin promotes energy storage; its absence favors breakdown of stored fat.
Correct. Without insulin, the body mobilizes fat and protein despite abundant circulating glucose.
Hepatic glucose production rises in insulin deficiency and contributes to hyperglycemia.

questions.takeaway: Absolute insulin deficiency creates a catabolic state with lipolysis, proteolysis, and weight loss.

questions.objective: Recognize diabetic ketoacidosis
questions.stem: A teenager has polyuria, vomiting, abdominal pain, dehydration, and deep rapid respirations. Glucose is 480 mg/dL, bicarbonate is low, and the anion gap is elevated. Which diagnosis best unifies the findings?

options.explanation: Correct. Hyperglycemia, ketone-related anion-gap acidosis, dehydration, and compensatory deep breathing form the classic DKA pattern.
HHS generally has extreme hyperglycemia and hyperosmolality with minimal ketoacidosis; this patient has clear anion-gap acidosis.
The rapid breathing is compensation for metabolic acidosis, not the primary disorder.
SIADH causes hypotonic hyponatremia and does not explain hyperglycemia with anion-gap acidosis.

questions.takeaway: DKA combines hyperglycemia, ketosis, anion-gap metabolic acidosis, and volume depletion.

questions.objective: Explain total-body potassium depletion in DKA
questions.stem: A patient with DKA has a serum potassium of 5.1 mEq/L before therapy. Which statement about potassium balance is most accurate?

options.text: Total-body potassium is increased because the serum value is elevated
options.explanation: The serum concentration does not reflect total-body stores in DKA; urinary losses usually produce depletion.

options.text: Total-body potassium is usually depleted despite a normal or elevated serum value
options.explanation: Correct. Insulin deficiency and acidosis shift potassium out of cells while osmotic diuresis removes potassium from the body.

options.text: Potassium will remain unchanged after insulin is started
options.explanation: Insulin drives potassium into cells, so the serum concentration can fall rapidly during treatment.

options.text: Urinary potassium loss is reduced by osmotic diuresis
options.explanation: Osmotic diuresis increases urinary water and electrolyte losses, including potassium.

questions.takeaway: DKA usually causes total-body potassium depletion even when initial serum potassium is normal or high.

questions.objective: Predict potassium response to insulin
questions.stem: Why can the serum potassium concentration fall quickly after insulin therapy begins in DKA?

options.text: Insulin shifts potassium from plasma into cells
options.explanation: Correct. Insulin activates cellular potassium uptake, unmasking the patient's underlying total-body potassium deficit.

options.text: Insulin directly blocks renal potassium reabsorption
options.explanation: The immediate fall is primarily a transcellular shift, not direct blockade of tubular reabsorption.

options.text: Insulin converts potassium into ketone bodies
options.explanation: Potassium is an electrolyte and is not converted into ketones.

options.text: Insulin raises the extracellular hydrogen ion concentration
options.explanation: Insulin treatment helps correct ketoacidosis; it does not lower potassium by worsening extracellular acidemia.

questions.takeaway: Insulin moves potassium intracellularly, making potassium measurement and replacement decisions central to DKA care.

questions.objective: Differentiate T2DM from T1DM
questions.stem: An adult with central adiposity and acanthosis nigricans has progressive hyperglycemia. Which combination best describes the usual pathophysiology of T2DM?

options.text: Autoimmune beta-cell destruction with absolute insulin deficiency
options.explanation: This is the core mechanism of T1DM.

options.text: Insulin resistance with progressive relative insulin deficiency
options.explanation: Correct. Tissues respond poorly to insulin, and beta-cell compensation eventually becomes inadequate.

options.text: Excess AVP secretion with renal water retention
options.explanation: This describes SIADH physiology and does not explain chronic hyperglycemia.
T2DM is not caused by isolated glucagon deficiency.

questions.takeaway: T2DM reflects insulin resistance combined with progressive beta-cell dysfunction.

questions.objective: Apply diabetes diagnostic criteria
questions.stem: A patient reports polyuria, polydipsia, and unexplained weight loss. A random plasma glucose is 242 mg/dL. Which interpretation is most appropriate?

options.text: The result supports a diagnosis of diabetes because classic symptoms accompany a random glucose at or above 200 mg/dL
options.explanation: Correct. Classic hyperglycemic symptoms plus a random plasma glucose at or above the diagnostic threshold supports diabetes.

options.text: The result is diagnostic only if the patient was fasting
options.explanation: A random glucose criterion does not require fasting when classic symptoms are present.

options.text: The result establishes prediabetes rather than diabetes
options.explanation: This value with classic symptoms meets a diabetes criterion, not merely a prediabetes range.

options.text: The result distinguishes T1DM from T2DM
options.explanation: The glucose establishes hyperglycemia but does not by itself classify the diabetes type.

questions.takeaway: Classic symptoms plus random plasma glucose of at least 200 mg/dL supports the diagnosis of diabetes but not its type.

citation.text: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026: Diagnosis and Classification of Diabetes

questions.objective: Differentiate HHS from DKA
questions.stem: An older adult with T2DM develops profound dehydration and altered mental status. Glucose is extremely elevated, serum osmolality is high, and ketones are minimal. Which diagnosis is most likely?

options.explanation: Correct. HHS is dominated by severe hyperglycemia, hyperosmolality, and dehydration with limited ketosis.
DKA is characterized by substantial ketone production and anion-gap metabolic acidosis.
AVP deficiency causes free-water loss and dilute urine but does not by itself produce extreme hyperglycemia.
Primary adrenal insufficiency more often causes hypotension, hyponatremia, and hyperkalemia rather than extreme hyperglycemia.

questions.takeaway: HHS features extreme hyperglycemia and hyperosmolality with profound dehydration and minimal ketoacidosis.

questions.objective: Calculate a meal bolus from carbohydrate coverage
questions.stem: A patient uses 1 unit of rapid-acting insulin for every 12 g of carbohydrate. The meal contains 60 g of carbohydrate, and no correction dose is needed. How much mealtime insulin is indicated by the prescribed ratio?

options.explanation: Three units would cover 36 g at this ratio, not 60 g.
Correct. Dividing 60 g by 12 g per unit gives 5 units.
The denominator describes grams covered by each unit; it is not itself the insulin dose.
Carbohydrate grams are not administered as an equal number of insulin units.

questions.takeaway: Carbohydrate-coverage dose equals carbohydrate grams divided by the insulin-to-carbohydrate ratio.

citation.text: Endotext: Insulin—Pharmacology, Therapeutic Regimens and Principles of Intensive Insulin Therapy

questions.objective: Calculate a hyperglycemia correction
questions.stem: A patient has a correction factor of 1 unit for each 40 mg/dL above a target of 120 mg/dL. Before lunch, glucose is 280 mg/dL. Ignoring carbohydrate coverage, what correction dose is indicated by the prescribed factor?

options.explanation: Two units would lower glucose by an estimated 80 mg/dL, leaving it above target.
Correct. The glucose is 160 mg/dL above target; 160 divided by 40 equals 4 units.
Dividing the current glucose directly by the correction factor ignores the target glucose.
The correction factor describes the expected glucose reduction per unit, not the number of units to administer.

questions.takeaway: Correction dose equals current glucose minus target glucose, divided by the correction factor.

citation.text: Endotext: Insulin—Pharmacology, Therapeutic Regimens and Principles of Intensive Insulin Therapy

questions.objective: Identify the insulin period associated with fasting hyperglycemia
questions.stem: For four consecutive days, a patient's glucose is near target at bedtime but elevated on waking. Continuous glucose data show a gradual rise overnight without an intervening low. Which part of the regimen should be evaluated most directly?

options.explanation: Breakfast insulin affects the post-breakfast and pre-lunch periods, not the preceding overnight rise.
The lunch correction factor does not act overnight.
Correct. A repeated rise from bedtime to morning without nocturnal hypoglycemia points to inadequate overnight basal coverage or another overnight factor.
A dinner mismatch can affect evening glucose, but the trace begins near target at bedtime and then rises gradually overnight.

questions.takeaway: Repeated fasting abnormalities should be interpreted from the overnight pattern before changing insulin.

citation.text: Endotext: Insulin—Pharmacology, Therapeutic Regimens and Principles of Intensive Insulin Therapy

questions.objective: Compare pump and injection regimens
questions.stem: Which feature most clearly distinguishes continuous subcutaneous insulin infusion from a basal-bolus injection regimen?

options.text: A pump delivers rapid-acting insulin for both basal delivery and meal boluses
options.explanation: Correct. Pump therapy uses rapid-acting insulin continuously for basal needs and in discrete meal or correction boluses.

options.text: A pump eliminates the need for mealtime insulin
options.explanation: Meal boluses are still required with pump therapy.

options.text: A pump continues to provide long-acting insulin after an infusion interruption
options.explanation: Standard pump therapy does not contain a long-acting depot, so interruption can quickly remove basal insulin delivery.

options.text: A pump cannot vary basal insulin by time of day
options.explanation: The ability to program different basal rates is a major advantage of pump therapy.

questions.takeaway: Insulin pumps generally use rapid-acting insulin for programmable basal delivery and boluses.

questions.objective: Recognize the practical consequences of NPH action
questions.stem: Compared with a relatively peakless long-acting basal analog, which feature of NPH most affects meal and snack planning?

options.text: It has a pronounced peak that can increase hypoglycemia risk
options.explanation: Correct. NPH has a clinically meaningful peak, so food and activity timing may need to account for it.

options.text: It begins working only after several days
options.explanation: NPH begins acting within hours, not days.

options.text: It can be used only in an insulin pump
options.explanation: Pumps generally use rapid-acting insulin; NPH is administered by injection.

options.text: It provides mealtime carbohydrate coverage without another insulin
options.explanation: NPH is intermediate acting and is not a direct substitute for rapid mealtime coverage.

questions.takeaway: The NPH peak makes timing of meals, snacks, and activity more consequential.

questions.objective: Recognize characteristic papillary carcinoma pathology
questions.stem: Fine-needle aspiration of a thyroid nodule shows enlarged nuclei with central clearing, nuclear grooves, and intranuclear cytoplasmic inclusions. Which additional finding would most strongly support the same diagnosis?

options.explanation: Amyloid stroma is characteristic of medullary thyroid carcinoma, which arises from parafollicular C cells.
Correct. Papillary carcinoma classically shows optically clear nuclei, nuclear grooves, intranuclear inclusions, and laminated calcifications called psammoma bodies.

options.text: Capsular and vascular invasion without papillary nuclear features
options.explanation: Capsular or vascular invasion is the defining malignant feature of follicular carcinoma.

options.text: Sheets of highly pleomorphic spindle and giant cells
options.explanation: Marked pleomorphism with spindle or giant cells suggests anaplastic carcinoma.

questions.takeaway: Papillary carcinoma is identified by its nuclear features and may contain psammoma bodies.

questions.objective: Distinguish aggressive thyroid carcinoma types
questions.stem: A 78-year-old develops a rapidly enlarging, hard thyroid mass with hoarseness, stridor, and local invasion. Biopsy shows highly pleomorphic undifferentiated cells. Which diagnosis is most likely?

options.explanation: Papillary carcinoma usually has distinctive nuclear clearing and grooves and generally has an excellent prognosis.
Follicular carcinoma is defined by capsular or vascular invasion and does not typically present as a rapidly invasive pleomorphic mass.
Medullary carcinoma is a calcitonin-producing neuroendocrine tumor with amyloid stroma.
Correct. Anaplastic carcinoma occurs mainly in older adults and presents as a rapidly enlarging, locally invasive mass composed of undifferentiated pleomorphic cells.

questions.takeaway: Anaplastic carcinoma is an aggressive tumor of older adults that often presents with rapid local compression and invasion.

questions.objective: Interpret thyrotoxicosis caused by thyroid hormone ingestion
questions.stem: A patient secretly takes high-dose levothyroxine for weight loss. Which combination is most likely?

options.text: High TSH with high radioactive iodine uptake
options.explanation: Exogenous thyroid hormone suppresses TSH and endogenous thyroid activity rather than increasing both.

options.text: Low TSH with low radioactive iodine uptake
options.explanation: Correct. Exogenous hormone produces thyrotoxicosis while suppressing TSH and the gland's own iodine uptake.

options.text: High TSH with low free T4
options.explanation: This is the classic pattern of primary hypothyroidism, not excess levothyroxine exposure.

options.text: Normal TSH with diffusely increased uptake
options.explanation: Diffuse increased uptake with suppressed TSH is more consistent with Graves disease; normal TSH would be inappropriate in overt thyrotoxicosis.

questions.takeaway: Exogenous thyroid hormone causes biochemical thyrotoxicosis but suppresses endogenous gland activity and radioactive iodine uptake.

questions.objective: Connect prolactin excess with reproductive and mass-effect findings
questions.stem: A patient has amenorrhea, galactorrhea, headaches, and difficulty seeing objects approaching from either side. Pregnancy testing is negative. Which laboratory abnormality is most likely?

options.explanation: Correct. A prolactinoma can produce amenorrhea and galactorrhea; a sufficiently large lesion can compress the optic chiasm and impair temporal visual fields.

options.text: Elevated free T4 with suppressed prolactin
options.explanation: This pattern would not unify galactorrhea with a sellar mass effect.
Aldosterone excess causes hypertension and hypokalemia, not galactorrhea and bitemporal visual loss.

options.text: Suppressed IGF-1 as the sole abnormality
options.explanation: Isolated GH-axis dysfunction does not explain galactorrhea; the reproductive findings point more directly to prolactin excess.

questions.takeaway: Amenorrhea and galactorrhea suggest prolactin excess; visual-field symptoms suggest a macroadenoma with chiasmal compression.

questions.objective: Explain dopamine-antagonist effects on prolactin
questions.stem: A patient develops galactorrhea and menstrual irregularity after beginning a dopamine D2-receptor-blocking antipsychotic. Which physiologic change most directly causes these effects?

options.text: Removal of tonic dopamine inhibition of lactotrophs
options.explanation: Correct. Dopamine normally restrains prolactin secretion; D2 blockade removes that inhibition and raises prolactin.

options.text: Direct activation of growth hormone receptors
options.explanation: D2 blockade does not directly stimulate GH receptors.
TRH can stimulate prolactin, but suppression of TRH would not explain medication-induced prolactin elevation.
The elevated prolactin arises from pituitary lactotroph disinhibition, not renal hormone synthesis.

questions.takeaway: D2 antagonists increase prolactin because dopamine normally inhibits lactotroph secretion.

questions.objective: Relate somatostatin analogs to GH excess treatment
questions.stem: A patient with acromegaly is not ready to undergo definitive pituitary surgery and begins a somatostatin analog. Which drug class effect is being used?

options.text: Stimulation of pituitary growth hormone release
options.explanation: Somatostatin physiologically inhibits, rather than stimulates, GH release.
Correct. Somatostatin analogs such as octreotide or lanreotide reduce GH secretion and thereby lower IGF-1.
Acromegaly is a state of GH and IGF-1 excess, so IGF-1 replacement would be inappropriate.

options.text: Stimulation of dopamine release from the adrenal medulla
options.explanation: The therapeutic effect is exerted on GH secretion, not through adrenal dopamine release.

questions.takeaway: Somatostatin analogs treat acromegaly by suppressing GH secretion and reducing IGF-1 production.

questions.objective: Interpret respiratory findings in metabolic acidosis
questions.stem: A patient with DKA is breathing deeply and rapidly. Which explanation best accounts for this respiratory pattern?

options.text: Primary respiratory alkalosis caused the ketoacidosis
options.explanation: The respiratory change is compensatory; it does not initiate ketone production or the metabolic acidosis.

options.text: Hyperventilation lowers carbon dioxide to compensate for metabolic acidosis
options.explanation: Correct. Deep rapid breathing reduces carbon dioxide and partially compensates for the fall in bicarbonate and pH.

options.text: Pulmonary edema prevents carbon dioxide elimination
options.explanation: Impaired carbon dioxide elimination would cause respiratory acidosis, not compensatory hypocapnia.

options.text: Insulin excess directly stimulates the respiratory center
options.explanation: DKA results from insulin deficiency; the respiratory drive is generated by acidemia.

questions.takeaway: Kussmaul respirations are respiratory compensation for severe metabolic acidosis in DKA.

questions.objective: Trace the branch points of adrenal steroidogenesis and name the products of each zone
questions.stem: A schematic of adrenal steroidogenesis is being annotated. Cholesterol has just been delivered to the inner mitochondrial membrane and converted to pregnenolone. Which enzyme catalyzed that first, rate-limiting conversion?

options.explanation: Correct. CYP11A1 (also called cholesterol side-chain cleavage enzyme or 20,22-desmolase) cleaves the side chain of cholesterol to yield pregnenolone. This is the first committed enzymatic step, shared by every steroid hormone, which is why the branch points that follow determine which hormone a given cell makes.
CYP21A2 acts far downstream, hydroxylating progesterone to 11-deoxycorticosterone and 17α-hydroxyprogesterone to 11-deoxycortisol.

HSD3B2 acts after pregnenolone, converting Δ5 steroids (pregnenolone, 17α-hydroxypregnenolone, DHEA) to their Δ4 counterparts (progesterone, 17α-hydroxyprogesterone, androstenedione). It does not make pregnenolone.
CYP11B2 catalyzes the final three steps to aldosterone and is expressed only in the zona glomerulosa. It is the last enzyme of one branch, not the first of the pathway.

StAR shuttles cholesterol from the outer to the inner mitochondrial membrane, and that transport step is the rate-limiting and acutely regulated point of steroidogenesis — ACTH raises cAMP, which upregulates StAR transcription. But StAR is a transport protein, not an enzyme: it delivers the substrate rather than catalyzing the conversion.

questions.takeaway: StAR delivers cholesterol to the inner mitochondrial membrane; CYP11A1 then cleaves it to pregnenolone — the committed step common to every steroid hormone.

questions.objective: Compare and contrast the pathways and locations for synthesis of the different steroid hormones
questions.stem: In the human adrenal cortex, CYP17A1 (17α-hydroxylase/17,20-lyase) is essentially absent from the outermost cortical zone, whereas aldosterone synthase (CYP11B2) is expressed only in that same zone. Which conclusion follows most directly from this pattern of enzyme expression?

options.explanation: Cortisol requires only the 17α-hydroxylase activity of CYP17A1 (progesterone → 17α-hydroxyprogesterone). The 17,20-lyase activity is needed only to cleave the C17–C20 bond and generate androgens.

options.text: The zona glomerulosa is the principal source of adrenal androgens
options.explanation: Reversed. Adrenal androgens (DHEA and DHEA-sulfate) come from the zona reticularis, which expresses abundant CYP17A1 with strong 17,20-lyase activity plus sulfotransferase SULT2A1.

options.text: The zona reticularis converts circulating aldosterone into cortisol
options.explanation: No such conversion occurs. Each zone synthesizes its products de novo from cholesterol along the branch its enzyme complement permits.

options.text: The zona glomerulosa is the only cortical zone that can complete aldosterone synthesis, and it cannot make cortisol or androgens
options.explanation: Correct. Restricting CYP11B2 to the zona glomerulosa makes it the sole source of aldosterone, and the absence of CYP17A1 there blocks entry into both the cortisol and the androgen branches. Zonal enzyme expression, not a difference in substrate, is what makes each zone functionally distinct.

options.text: The zona fasciculata is the only zone capable of producing a mineralocorticoid effect
options.explanation: The zona fasciculata makes 11-deoxycorticosterone and corticosterone, which do have weak mineralocorticoid activity, but it lacks CYP11B2 and therefore cannot make aldosterone. The stem's premise points to the glomerulosa, not the fasciculata.

questions.takeaway: Zonation is enzyme expression: CYP11B2 only in glomerulosa (aldosterone), CYP17A1 only in fasciculata and reticularis (cortisol and androgens).

questions.objective: Explain why 17α-hydroxylase and 17,20-lyase activities of a single gene product have different consequences
questions.stem: 17α-hydroxylase and 17,20-lyase activities reside in a single polypeptide encoded by CYP17A1. A patient is found to carry a mutation that selectively abolishes 17,20-lyase activity while leaving 17α-hydroxylase activity intact. Which hormonal pattern is expected?

options.text: Cortisol production preserved; adrenal androgen production severely impaired
options.explanation: Correct. Cortisol requires only 17α-hydroxylation of progesterone to 17α-hydroxyprogesterone, after which 21-hydroxylase and 11β-hydroxylase finish the job. Generating DHEA and androstenedione requires the additional 17,20-lyase cleavage of the C17–C20 bond, so isolated lyase loss spares cortisol and eliminates androgens. The same logic explains normal zonation: 17,20-lyase activity depends on cytochrome B5, which is expressed in the zona reticularis but not the zona fasciculata — so the fasciculata performs the 17-hydroxylation without the subsequent cleavage and makes cortisol, while the reticularis proceeds to androgens.
CYP17A1 is not required for aldosterone synthesis at all — the zona glomerulosa does not express it. Aldosterone is unaffected by CYP17A1 mutations of either kind.

options.text: Both cortisol and adrenal androgens severely impaired
options.explanation: This is the pattern of complete combined 17α-hydroxylase/17,20-lyase deficiency, in which both activities of CYP17A1 are lost. The stem specifies that hydroxylase activity is intact.

options.text: Cortisol production severely impaired; adrenal androgen production preserved
options.explanation: This is the reverse. Androgen synthesis is the activity that depends on the lyase step, so androgens — not cortisol — are the ones lost.

options.text: Both cortisol and adrenal androgens increased
options.explanation: Loss of an enzymatic activity cannot increase flux through the step it catalyzes. ACTH will rise as cortisol falls, but here cortisol does not fall.

questions.takeaway: One gene, two activities: 17α-hydroxylase alone suffices for cortisol, but adrenal androgens additionally require the 17,20-lyase activity of the same CYP17A1 protein.

questions.objective: Formulate a mechanism by which 21-hydroxylase deficiency gives rise to atypical genitalia in 46,XX infants
questions.stem: A term newborn with a 46,XX karyotype has clitoromegaly and partially fused labioscrotal folds; no gonads are palpable. Serum 17α-hydroxyprogesterone is markedly elevated. Which mechanism best explains the appearance of the external genitalia?

options.text: Failure of peripheral conversion of testosterone to dihydrotestosterone
options.explanation: That is 5α-reductase deficiency, which undervirilizes a 46,XY fetus. It cannot virilize a 46,XX fetus, and it does not elevate 17α-hydroxyprogesterone.

options.text: Loss of negative feedback on LH driving fetal Leydig cell testosterone output
options.explanation: A 46,XX fetus with ovaries has no Leydig cells. The androgen source here is the hyperstimulated adrenal cortex.

options.text: Precursors accumulating above the enzyme block are diverted through 17,20-lyase into adrenal androgens
options.explanation: Correct. With CYP21A2 blocked, 17α-hydroxyprogesterone cannot proceed to 11-deoxycortisol. Cortisol falls, ACTH rises, the cortex hypertrophies, and the excess 17α-hydroxyprogesterone is shunted down the one open branch — through 17,20-lyase to androstenedione and testosterone — which virilizes the external genitalia of a 46,XX fetus during the critical first-trimester window.

options.text: Placental aromatase deficiency permitting maternal androgens to reach the fetus
options.explanation: Aromatase deficiency is a genuine cause of 46,XX virilization, but it is a separate disorder: it presents with maternal virilization during pregnancy and does not raise 17α-hydroxyprogesterone.

options.text: Autonomous aldosterone secretion by a hyperplastic zona glomerulosa
options.explanation: 21-hydroxylase deficiency blocks the mineralocorticoid branch as well, so aldosterone is deficient, not excessive — and aldosterone does not virilize.

questions.takeaway: In 21-hydroxylase deficiency the blocked cortisol pathway drives ACTH up and shunts accumulated 17α-hydroxyprogesterone into adrenal androgens — the cause of 46,XX virilization.

questions.objective: Explain why classic 21-hydroxylase deficiency produces both glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid failure
questions.stem: A 3-week-old infant with an abnormal newborn screen presents with vomiting, poor weight gain, and lethargy. Blood pressure is 58/30 mm Hg. Sodium is 124 mEq/L, potassium 6.7 mEq/L, and glucose 44 mg/dL. Deficiency of which pair of hormones best accounts for this combination of findings?

options.explanation: Isolated glucocorticoid deficiency (as in ACTH deficiency) causes hypoglycemia and hyponatremia but characteristically spares potassium, because aldosterone is driven by angiotensin II and potassium rather than by ACTH.
DHT is a peripheral product of 5α-reductase and has no role in sodium, potassium, or glucose homeostasis.

Isolated aldosterone synthase deficiency does produce salt wasting with hyperkalemia, but it leaves cortisol intact and so would not explain the hypoglycemia; nor would it raise 17α-hydroxyprogesterone on the newborn screen.

Correct. CYP21A2 is required on both arms of the pathway: progesterone → 11-deoxycorticosterone (mineralocorticoid arm) and 17α-hydroxyprogesterone → 11-deoxycortisol (glucocorticoid arm). Losing aldosterone gives hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, and hypovolemic shock; losing cortisol gives hypoglycemia and impaired vascular tone.
Adrenal androgen synthesis does not require 21-hydroxylase and is in fact increased in this disorder. DHEA deficiency would not cause hypoglycemia.

questions.takeaway: Classic salt-wasting CAH is simultaneous cortisol and aldosterone failure with androgen excess — 21-hydroxylase sits on both the glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid arms.

questions.objective: Compare 21-hydroxylase and 11β-hydroxylase deficiency using blood pressure and potassium
questions.stem: A 3-year-old with a 46,XX karyotype has clitoromegaly, pubic hair, and a height at the 97th percentile. Blood pressure is 118/78 mm Hg (above the 99th percentile for age). Sodium is 146 mEq/L and potassium is 3.1 mEq/L. Serum 11-deoxycortisol and 11-deoxycorticosterone are markedly elevated. Which enzyme is deficient?

options.explanation: Correct. CYP11B1 converts 11-deoxycortisol to cortisol and 11-deoxycorticosterone to corticosterone. When it is blocked, cortisol falls and ACTH rises (driving androgen excess and virilization), while 11-deoxycorticosterone accumulates. Because 11-deoxycorticosterone is itself an agonist at the mineralocorticoid receptor, the result is hypertension with hypokalemic alkalosis rather than salt wasting.
Isolated CYP11B2 deficiency causes salt wasting with hyperkalemia and no virilization, since cortisol and androgen synthesis are untouched.

21-hydroxylase deficiency also virilizes a 46,XX child, but it blocks the pathway upstream of 11-deoxycorticosterone, so mineralocorticoid activity is lost — giving hypotension, hyponatremia, and hyperkalemia, the opposite of this patient's electrolytes.
HSD3B2 deficiency impairs all three classes of steroid, giving salt wasting with only weak virilization from DHEA. It does not raise 11-deoxycortisol and does not cause hypertension.

CYP17A1 deficiency also causes hypertension and hypokalemia from 11-deoxycorticosterone excess, but it blocks sex-steroid synthesis — producing absent virilization and absent puberty, not clitoromegaly and pubic hair.

questions.takeaway: Both 21- and 11β-hydroxylase deficiency virilize 46,XX infants; blood pressure and potassium separate them — 21-OHD wastes salt, 11β-OHD retains it via 11-deoxycorticosterone.

questions.objective: Recognize combined 17α-hydroxylase/17,20-lyase deficiency from hypertension plus absent sex steroids
questions.stem: A 16-year-old raised as a girl is evaluated for primary amenorrhea. There has been no breast development and no pubic or axillary hair. External genitalia appear female. Blood pressure is 160/100 mm Hg and serum potassium is 2.8 mEq/L. Which enzyme deficiency best explains this combination?

options.explanation: Aldosterone synthase deficiency causes hypotension, hyponatremia, and hyperkalemia, and leaves sexual development normal.

5α-reductase deficiency affects only conversion of testosterone to dihydrotestosterone in a 46,XY individual. It does not affect blood pressure or potassium, and testosterone-driven virilization occurs at puberty.

11β-hydroxylase deficiency does cause hypertension with hypokalemia, but ACTH-driven androgen production is intact and increased, so patients virilize instead of failing to develop any secondary sexual characteristics.

Correct. Loss of CYP17A1 blocks both cortisol and all sex steroids, so there is neither gonadal nor adrenal androgen or estrogen production — hence no breast development and no pubic hair. Meanwhile ACTH drives the one remaining open branch, accumulating 11-deoxycorticosterone and corticosterone, whose mineralocorticoid activity produces hypertension with hypokalemic alkalosis and suppressed renin.
21-hydroxylase deficiency causes androgen excess and salt wasting — hypotension and hyperkalemia, with virilization rather than absent sexual development.

questions.takeaway: Hypertension plus hypokalemia plus complete absence of pubertal sex steroids is the signature of 17α-hydroxylase deficiency: mineralocorticoid precursors accumulate while every sex steroid is lost.

questions.objective: Dissect the molecular basis and etymology of glucocorticoid-remediable hyperaldosteronism
questions.stem: Three generations of a family have hypertension beginning in childhood, mild hypokalemia, and suppressed plasma renin with an elevated aldosterone-to-renin ratio. Aldosterone output tracks the diurnal rhythm of ACTH rather than responding to posture or sodium loading, and both blood pressure and aldosterone normalize on low-dose dexamethasone. Which molecular event best explains this disorder?

options.explanation: Apparent mineralocorticoid excess lets cortisol occupy the mineralocorticoid receptor. Aldosterone is low, the urinary cortisol-to-cortisone ratio is elevated, and hybrid steroids are not formed.

options.text: Activating mutation of the mineralocorticoid receptor
options.explanation: A constitutively active mineralocorticoid receptor causes hypertension with hypokalemia, but aldosterone would be low (the receptor needs no ligand), and dexamethasone would not help.

options.text: Gain-of-function mutation in the epithelial sodium channel
options.explanation: That is Liddle syndrome. Renin and aldosterone are both suppressed, hybrid steroids are absent, and the treatment is amiloride or triamterene, not a glucocorticoid.
A sporadic adenoma does not follow autosomal dominant inheritance across three generations and is not suppressible by dexamethasone; it is treated by adrenalectomy.

options.text: Unequal crossing over between CYP11B1 and CYP11B2 producing a chimeric gene in which aldosterone synthase activity is driven by the ACTH-responsive CYP11B1 promoter
options.explanation: Correct. CYP11B2 arose from CYP11B1 by gene duplication, the two genes sit adjacent on chromosome 8, and the regions encoding 11β-hydroxylase activity are about 97% identical — which makes them prone to unequal crossing over during meiotic recombination. That is the "design flaw" that permits this disease. The resulting chimera places aldosterone synthase coding sequence under the ACTH-responsive CYP11B1 promoter and expresses it in the zona fasciculata, so aldosterone secretion now follows ACTH. Suppressing ACTH with low-dose dexamethasone therefore switches the aldosterone off — the "glucocorticoid-remediable" half of the name. The reciprocal chimera, which puts 11β-hydroxylase under angiotensin II control, is clinically silent because normal cortisol output vastly exceeds normal aldosterone output.

questions.takeaway: Familial (glucocorticoid-remediable) hyperaldosteronism: a CYP11B1/CYP11B2 chimera puts aldosterone synthase under the ACTH-driven CYP11B1 promoter, so aldosterone follows ACTH and remits on low-dose dexamethasone.

questions.objective: Localize cortisol overproduction to the correct cortical zone
questions.stem: A 55-year-old man has centripetal weight gain, wide violaceous abdominal striae, thin skin that bruises easily, and proximal muscle weakness. Twenty-four-hour urinary free cortisol is markedly elevated. Overproduction of the responsible hormone occurs in which layer of the adrenal gland?

options.explanation: The zona glomerulosa lacks CYP17A1 and makes aldosterone. Aldosterone excess causes hypertension with hypokalemia, not striae, thin skin, and proximal myopathy.
The capsule is connective tissue and is not steroidogenic.
Chromaffin cells of the medulla secrete catecholamines, which cause paroxysmal hypertension, headache, and diaphoresis.

Correct. The zona fasciculata is the thick middle layer of lipid-rich, cord-arranged cells that expresses CYP17A1, CYP21A2, and CYP11B1 and is the principal site of cortisol synthesis under ACTH control. Cortisol excess produces exactly this constellation — catabolic skin and muscle changes, central fat redistribution, and striae.
The innermost cortical zone makes DHEA and DHEA-sulfate. Androgen excess causes hirsutism, acne, and virilization rather than the catabolic features described.

questions.takeaway: Cortisol is a zona fasciculata product; its excess shows up as catabolic skin, muscle, and fat-distribution changes.

questions.objective: Identify the hormones produced by the innermost cortical zone
questions.stem: A photomicrograph of the adrenal gland is examined. The zone identified lies immediately internal to the thick, cord-like middle layer and directly abuts the medulla; its cells are compact, contain lipofuscin pigment, and are arranged in an anastomosing network. Which hormones do the predominant cells of this zone secrete?

options.explanation: Correct. This describes the zona reticularis. Its high 17,20-lyase activity and expression of the sulfotransferase SULT2A1 make it the source of DHEA and DHEA-sulfate, the principal adrenal androgens, which serve as peripheral precursors for testosterone and estrogens.

Catecholamines come from chromaffin cells of the medulla, which is internal to — not part of — the cortex. Cortisol draining from the cortex is in fact what induces the medullary enzyme that makes epinephrine.
Aldosterone comes from the zona glomerulosa, the outermost zone just beneath the capsule, where cells form small rounded clusters.
Cortisol comes from the zona fasciculata, which is the thick lipid-rich middle layer described in the stem as lying external to the zone in question.
Renin is produced by juxtaglomerular cells of the kidney, not by the adrenal gland.

questions.takeaway: Capsule inward: glomerulosa (aldosterone), fasciculata (cortisol), reticularis (DHEA/DHEA-S), medulla (catecholamines).

questions.objective: Prescribe the correct first-line diagnostic test for suspected primary hyperaldosteronism
questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman has blood pressure of 172/108 mm Hg despite three antihypertensive agents at full dose. She reports muscle weakness and nocturia. Sodium is 145 mEq/L, potassium 2.9 mEq/L, and bicarbonate 32 mEq/L. Which is the most appropriate initial test?

options.explanation: Adrenal vein sampling is a subtype study used to distinguish a unilateral adenoma from bilateral hyperplasia — that is, to decide between surgery and medical therapy. It comes after the diagnosis is biochemically confirmed, not before.

options.text: Plasma aldosterone concentration and plasma renin activity, reported as a ratio
options.explanation: Correct. Resistant hypertension with spontaneous hypokalemia and metabolic alkalosis is the classic screening indication for primary aldosteronism. The aldosterone-to-renin ratio is the recommended first step: it is high because autonomous aldosterone secretion expands volume and suppresses renin. Confirmatory testing (saline suppression or oral sodium loading) follows a positive screen.

Pheochromocytoma is worth considering in resistant hypertension, but it typically presents with paroxysmal headache, palpitations, and diaphoresis, and it does not cause hypokalemic alkalosis with a suppressed renin.

Cortisol excess can cause hypertension and hypokalemia, but this patient has none of the catabolic features — striae, thin skin, proximal myopathy, central fat redistribution — that would prompt screening for Cushing syndrome first.

Imaging is also a localization step, and it is unreliable on its own: nonfunctioning incidentalomas are common and small aldosterone-producing adenomas are often missed. Confirm the hormone excess before imaging.

questions.takeaway: Screen resistant hypertension with hypokalemia using the aldosterone-to-renin ratio; confirm biochemically, then localize with CT and adrenal vein sampling.

questions.objective: Distinguish primary from secondary hyperaldosteronism
questions.stem: A 64-year-old man with coronary artery disease presents with worsening leg edema. Blood pressure is 190/110 mm Hg. Sodium is 146 mEq/L and potassium is 3.0 mEq/L. Duplex ultrasonography shows 80% stenosis of the right renal artery. Compared with a patient who has an aldosterone-producing adrenal adenoma, which finding is expected in this man?

options.explanation: Aldosterone is elevated in both conditions; that is why hypokalemia and alkalosis appear in each. The discriminator is renin, not aldosterone.
Hyperkalemia is a feature of aldosterone deficiency or mineralocorticoid receptor blockade. This patient is hypokalemic, as the stem states.

options.text: Plasma renin activity is elevated rather than suppressed
options.explanation: Correct. Renal artery stenosis reduces perfusion pressure at the juxtaglomerular apparatus, which drives renin release; angiotensin II then stimulates aldosterone synthesis in the zona glomerulosa. Aldosterone excess is therefore secondary to — and downstream of — high renin, so renin is normal or high. In primary aldosteronism the autonomous aldosterone expands volume and suppresses renin instead. The two conditions separate cleanly on renin, which is why the screening test is a ratio rather than an aldosterone level alone.

options.text: Metabolic acidosis rather than metabolic alkalosis
options.explanation: Mineralocorticoid excess of either cause increases distal sodium reabsorption in exchange for potassium and hydrogen ion, producing hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis in both.
ACTH is not the trophic driver of aldosterone in either disorder and is not the axis being tested here.

questions.takeaway: Aldosterone is high in both; renin sorts them out — suppressed in primary aldosteronism, elevated in secondary (renal artery stenosis, renin-secreting tumor, heart failure, cirrhosis).

questions.objective: Prescribe the correct first-line diagnostic test for suspected cortisol excess
questions.stem: A 45-year-old man with hypertension treated with hydrochlorothiazide reports weight gain, increased thirst and urination, and one day of severe low back pain that began while lifting a suitcase. Examination shows fat accumulation over the lower posterior neck and point tenderness over the lumbar spine; straight-leg raise is negative bilaterally. Which is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis?

options.explanation: Imaging before biochemical confirmation is the classic error. Adrenal incidentalomas are found in several percent of adults, so a mass discovered at this stage would not establish that it is the source of anything.
ACTH is the right test for the second step — separating ACTH-dependent from ACTH-independent disease — but it is uninterpretable until cortisol excess has actually been demonstrated.

Correct. Central weight gain, a dorsocervical fat pad, new glucose intolerance, and a low-trauma vertebral compression fracture together suggest endogenous hypercortisolism. The first step is always to establish cortisol excess biochemically, using any of three accepted screens: 24-hour urinary free cortisol, late-night salivary cortisol, or the 1-mg overnight dexamethasone suppression test.
Pituitary imaging is a late localizing step reserved for confirmed ACTH-dependent hypercortisolism, and small corticotroph adenomas are frequently not visible.
This will document the hyperglycemia but explains neither the fat redistribution nor the fragility fracture, and it does not test the underlying hypothesis.

questions.takeaway: Cushing workup has a fixed order: prove cortisol excess (24-h UFC, late-night salivary cortisol, or 1-mg DST), then measure ACTH to find the level, then image.

questions.objective: Use ACTH to localize the cause of hypercortisolism
questions.stem: A 54-year-old woman has new type 2 diabetes, osteoporosis, hypertension, weight gain, and abdominal striae. Twenty-four-hour urinary free cortisol is elevated and cortisol fails to suppress on an overnight dexamethasone suppression test. Plasma ACTH is less than 10 pg/mL (reference 10–60). CT of the abdomen shows a single 3-cm mass adjacent to the upper pole of the right kidney. Which is the most likely explanation?

options.explanation: Exogenous steroid does suppress ACTH, but it also suppresses endogenous cortisol — urinary free cortisol would be low, both adrenals would be atrophic, and there would be no mass.

options.text: Ectopic ACTH secretion by a small cell lung carcinoma
options.explanation: Ectopic ACTH is also ACTH-dependent, with high ACTH and bilateral adrenal hyperplasia. It typically presents more abruptly with severe hypokalemia and marked hyperpigmentation.
This is another ACTH-independent cause and would also show a suppressed ACTH, but by definition the abnormality is bilateral and nodular, not a single mass with an atrophic contralateral gland.

Correct. Cortisol produced autonomously by an adrenal tumor feeds back on the pituitary and suppresses ACTH. A suppressed ACTH therefore places the lesion at the adrenal itself rather than above it, and the unilateral mass identifies which adrenal. This is ACTH-independent (primary adrenal) Cushing syndrome, treated by unilateral adrenalectomy.

options.text: Corticotroph adenoma of the pituitary (Cushing disease)
options.explanation: Cushing disease is ACTH-dependent: ACTH would be normal or elevated rather than undetectable, and the adrenal glands would be diffusely enlarged rather than harboring a single mass.

questions.takeaway: Suppressed ACTH means the adrenal is the driver. Unilateral mass plus contralateral atrophy points to a cortisol-secreting adenoma; low cortisol with low ACTH means exogenous steroid instead.

questions.objective: Distinguish pituitary from ectopic sources of ACTH-dependent hypercortisolism
questions.stem: A 38-year-old woman has biochemically confirmed hypercortisolism with a plasma ACTH of 118 pg/mL (elevated). Which additional finding would most strongly favor a pituitary corticotroph adenoma over ectopic ACTH secretion?

options.text: Severe hypokalemia with onset of symptoms over roughly six weeks
options.explanation: Rapid onset with profound hypokalemic alkalosis and weight loss instead suggests an ectopic, often malignant, source producing very high ACTH.
Bilateral hyperplasia is the expected consequence of any sustained ACTH excess, pituitary or ectopic, so it does not localize the source.

options.text: Failure of cortisol to suppress after low-dose (1 mg) dexamethasone
options.explanation: Low-dose non-suppression is a second-line test used to establish that Cushing syndrome is present at all. It is shared by every ACTH-dependent and ACTH-independent cause, so it discriminates nothing about the source.
Hyperpigmentation reflects the magnitude of proopiomelanocortin-derived peptide excess and is more pronounced with the very high ACTH levels of ectopic secretion.

options.text: Cortisol suppresses substantially on a high-dose dexamethasone suppression test
options.explanation: Correct. This is exactly what the high-dose dexamethasone suppression test is for. Corticotroph adenomas retain partial glucocorticoid feedback sensitivity, so a high dose still suppresses them; ectopic ACTH-secreting tumors and adrenal tumors do not suppress. That is the third-line test in the Cushing algorithm, used only after cortisol excess is confirmed and ACTH has established that the disease is ACTH-dependent. (A CRH stimulation test and, when biochemistry stays equivocal, bilateral inferior petrosal sinus sampling can settle the remaining hard cases.)

questions.takeaway: Both pituitary and ectopic Cushing have high ACTH; high-dose dexamethasone suppression plus a CRH response favor pituitary, and petrosal sinus sampling settles hard cases.

questions.objective: Associate the findings of primary adrenal insufficiency with the underlying hormone deficiencies
questions.stem: A 34-year-old man reports six months of progressive fatigue, unintentional weight loss, and intense craving for salty foods. Blood pressure is 92/45 mm Hg. There is hyperpigmentation of the buccal mucosa, palmar creases, and knuckles. Sodium is 128 mEq/L, potassium 5.9 mEq/L, and fasting glucose 62 mg/dL. Which laboratory value is most likely to be elevated?

options.explanation: Correct. Destruction of the adrenal cortex removes cortisol negative feedback, so corticotroph output of proopiomelanocortin-derived peptides rises. The excess ACTH stimulates melanocortin-1 receptors on melanocytes, which is why hyperpigmentation appears specifically at sun-exposed skin, pressure points, scars, palmar creases, and mucosa — and why it occurs in primary but not secondary adrenal insufficiency.
Aldosterone deficiency reduces distal hydrogen ion secretion, so a mild hyperkalemic metabolic acidosis with a low bicarbonate is typical.
DHEA-sulfate comes from the zona reticularis and falls along with the rest of the cortex; low DHEA-S is a supportive finding in autoimmune adrenalitis.
Aldosterone is deficient here — that is the cause of the hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, salt craving, and hypotension.
Cortisol is low; the hypoglycemia and poor vascular tone are direct consequences. A morning cortisol that fails to rise after cosyntropin confirms it.

questions.takeaway: Primary adrenal insufficiency = loss of cortisol AND aldosterone with a compensatory ACTH rise; the ACTH excess is what pigments the skin and mucosa.

questions.objective: Recognize adrenal crisis precipitated by stopping replacement therapy
questions.stem: A 45-year-old man with a several-month history of nausea and light-headedness comes to clinic with severe back pain, diffuse muscle weakness, and fatigue. The buccal mucosa is darkly pigmented and systolic blood pressure is 94 mm Hg. He mentions that he stopped taking a medication for a chronic condition a few weeks ago because he felt it was not helping. Sodium is 127 mEq/L, potassium 6.0 mEq/L, and glucose 56 mg/dL. Which medication did he most likely discontinue?

options.explanation: Azoles inhibit steroidogenic cytochrome P450 enzymes, so high-dose azole therapy can *cause* adrenal insufficiency. Stopping it would improve adrenal function, not precipitate crisis.
Stopping metformin causes hyperglycemia, not hypoglycemia, and produces no hyperpigmentation, hyperkalemia, or hypotension.
DHEA is at most an adjunct for libido and well-being in adrenal insufficiency. It has no glucocorticoid or mineralocorticoid activity and stopping it does not cause crisis.
Withdrawal of levothyroxine causes hypothyroid symptoms — fatigue, constipation, cold intolerance, weight gain — and can cause hyponatremia, but not hyperkalemia or mucosal pigmentation.

Correct. Hyperpigmented mucosa indicates chronic ACTH excess, meaning he has primary adrenal insufficiency and had been on glucocorticoid replacement. Withdrawing it removes the only source of cortisol in a gland that cannot make its own, precipitating crisis: hypotension, hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, and hypoglycemia. Treatment is immediate intravenous hydrocortisone plus isotonic saline with dextrose — given before confirmatory testing returns.

questions.takeaway: Any patient with treated primary adrenal insufficiency who stops replacement is in crisis until proven otherwise — give IV hydrocortisone and saline first, test later.

questions.objective: Discuss why primary and secondary adrenal insufficiency differ in potassium and pigmentation
questions.stem: Two patients each have fatigue, orthostatic hypotension, hyponatremia, and a low 8 AM cortisol that fails to rise after cosyntropin. The first has potassium 6.1 mEq/L, hyperpigmented palmar creases, and ACTH of 940 pg/mL. The second has potassium 4.1 mEq/L, pale skin, and ACTH of 5 pg/mL. Which principle best explains why hyperkalemia occurs in the first patient but not the second?

options.text: ACTH is the principal trophic stimulus for aldosterone secretion
options.explanation: If this were true, patient 2 would also be hyperkalemic. Chronic ACTH deficiency does cause some glomerulosa atrophy, but aldosterone responsiveness to volume depletion is largely retained.

options.text: The second patient has a coexisting mineralocorticoid excess state
options.explanation: There is nothing in the vignette to suggest this, and a normal potassium is exactly what isolated ACTH deficiency predicts on its own.

options.text: Aldosterone synthesis fails when the adrenal cortex itself is destroyed, but is preserved in ACTH deficiency because it is driven mainly by angiotensin II and potassium
options.explanation: Correct. ACTH is a permissive but minor regulator of the zona glomerulosa; the dominant stimuli are angiotensin II and serum potassium acting through an intact renin-angiotensin system. Destroying the cortex (patient 1) therefore removes aldosterone and produces hyperkalemia, whereas loss of pituitary ACTH (patient 2) leaves the glomerulosa functional. The same logic explains the pigmentation: only patient 1 has an ACTH excess to stimulate melanocytes.

options.text: Skin hyperpigmentation itself alters renal potassium handling
options.explanation: Hyperpigmentation is a downstream marker of ACTH excess with no effect on renal transport.

options.text: Cortisol acts directly on the collecting duct to promote potassium secretion
options.explanation: Cortisol can occupy the mineralocorticoid receptor when 11β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase type 2 is overwhelmed, but this is not the mechanism separating the two patients — both are cortisol deficient, yet only one is hyperkalemic.

questions.takeaway: Hyperkalemia and hyperpigmentation are the two features that mark adrenal insufficiency as primary; ACTH deficiency spares aldosterone because angiotensin II and potassium drive it.

questions.objective: Recognize acute hemorrhagic adrenal failure and its usual pathogen
questions.stem: A 20-year-old college student is brought to the emergency department after acutely developing confusion, fever, nausea, and vomiting. She is febrile, hypotensive, and disoriented, with flank and abdominal tenderness and a rapidly spreading petechial rash. CT shows bilateral adrenal hemorrhage. Which organism best accounts for these findings?

options.explanation: Streptococcus pneumoniae can cause purpura fulminans and adrenal hemorrhage, particularly in asplenic patients, but it is a much less common cause than meningococcus in a previously healthy young adult with this presentation.
Histoplasma capsulatum likewise causes chronic granulomatous adrenal destruction, usually in disseminated disease in an immunocompromised host, over weeks to months.

Correct. This is Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome, in which fulminant Neisseria meningitidis bacteremia causes disseminated intravascular coagulation and hemorrhagic infarction of both adrenal glands. The adrenal medulla's single-vein drainage and sinusoidal architecture make it especially vulnerable. The result is abrupt loss of cortisol and aldosterone superimposed on septic shock — which is why empiric stress-dose glucocorticoid accompanies antibiotics and vasopressors.
Cytomegalovirus adrenalitis occurs in advanced HIV infection and causes gradual insufficiency, not acute bilateral hemorrhage with petechiae.

Mycobacterium tuberculosis is a major worldwide cause of primary adrenal insufficiency, but it destroys the glands slowly by caseating granulomatous inflammation, producing chronic insufficiency with calcified glands — not an acute hemorrhagic catastrophe.

questions.takeaway: Fulminant meningococcemia with DIC → bilateral adrenal hemorrhage (Waterhouse-Friderichsen) → acute primary adrenal failure; TB, Histoplasma, and CMV destroy the glands slowly instead.

questions.objective: Prescribe the correct first-line biochemical test for suspected pheochromocytoma
questions.stem: A 43-year-old woman describes several weeks of episodic pounding headache, drenching sweats, and palpitations. Blood pressure today is 185/105 mm Hg; a record from one year ago documents 125/80 mm Hg. Which is the most appropriate initial test?

options.explanation: This screens for primary aldosteronism, which causes sustained hypertension with hypokalemia rather than adrenergic paroxysms.

Correct. Chromaffin tumors metabolize catecholamines continuously within the tumor by membrane-bound catechol-O-methyltransferase, so metanephrines are elevated even between paroxysms. Plasma free metanephrines (or fractionated 24-hour urinary metanephrines) is therefore the recommended first-line test, with high sensitivity that makes a normal result strongly reassuring.
5-HIAA is the screening test for carcinoid syndrome, which causes flushing, diarrhea, and wheezing — and characteristically not hypertension.
Functional imaging is used to find extra-adrenal paraganglioma or metastatic disease after the biochemical diagnosis is established. It is not a screening test.
As with aldosteronism, confirm the hormone excess before imaging — otherwise an incidental adrenal nodule will be misattributed.

questions.takeaway: Suspect pheochromocytoma on episodic headache, palpitations, and diaphoresis with new hypertension; screen with plasma free metanephrines, then image.

questions.objective: Discuss preoperative management of pheochromocytoma
questions.stem: A 43-year-old man has elevated urinary metanephrines and a 5-cm left adrenal mass. Laparoscopic adrenalectomy is planned. Which preoperative regimen is most appropriate?

options.text: Metoprolol for two weeks, then phenoxybenzamine on the day of surgery
options.explanation: This has the sequence backwards, and cardioselectivity does not make early β-blockade safe in an unblocked patient.

options.text: Phenylephrine to maintain blood pressure during induction
options.explanation: Phenylephrine is an α1 agonist — exactly the wrong direction. Vasopressors may be needed after tumor removal, once the catecholamine source is gone, but not as preparation.

options.text: A phentolamine infusion begun in the operating room, with no oral preparation
options.explanation: Phentolamine is a short-acting intravenous α-blocker used for intraoperative surges and hypertensive emergencies. It cannot substitute for the days of oral α-blockade needed to restore intravascular volume.

options.text: α-adrenergic blockade with phenoxybenzamine first, adding a β-blocker later only if tachycardia persists
options.explanation: Correct. Blood pressure must be normalized with an α-adrenergic receptor blocker before any β-blocker is introduced, and adequate α-blockade also lets the chronically contracted intravascular volume re-expand — which is why liberal salt and fluid intake accompanies it and why preparation takes days to a couple of weeks rather than hours. Surgery remains high risk and needs an experienced surgical and anesthesia team.

Blocking β2-mediated vasodilation while α receptors remain unopposed leaves catecholamines acting on α1 alone — the classic route to a hypertensive crisis. β-blockade before α-blockade is the error the question is built around.

questions.takeaway: α before β: normalize blood pressure with phenoxybenzamine (plus salt and volume repletion) first, then add a β-blocker for residual tachycardia. β-blocker monotherapy risks hypertensive crisis from unopposed α stimulation.

questions.objective: Recognize MEN1 from its characteristic tumor combination and inheritance
questions.stem: A 30-year-old man reports seven months of fatigue, weight loss, depression, and epigastric pain that improves after eating. He has passed two kidney stones in the past year and reports declining libido. Serum calcium is 11.6 mg/dL and parathyroid hormone is 760 pg/mL. He was adopted and does not know his family history. Which diagnosis best fits, and how is it inherited?

options.text: Multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2A; gain-of-function of the RET proto-oncogene
options.explanation: MEN2A does include hyperparathyroidism, but its defining lesions are medullary thyroid carcinoma and pheochromocytoma — neither suggested here — and it does not cause pancreatic or pituitary tumors.
A single sporadic adenoma would not be accompanied by a gastrinoma and a pituitary lesion in a 30-year-old.

options.text: Multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1; autosomal dominant loss-of-function of the MEN1 tumor suppressor
options.explanation: Correct. Primary hyperparathyroidism from multigland parathyroid hyperplasia is usually the first and most penetrant manifestation of MEN1, and it combines here with a gastrin-secreting pancreatic tumor (ulcer pain relieved by food) and a pituitary lesion suggested by the reduced libido — the classic parathyroid, pancreas, pituitary triad. MEN1 encodes menin, a tumor suppressor, so inheritance is autosomal dominant with a somatic second hit.

options.text: Multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2B; gain-of-function of the RET proto-oncogene
options.explanation: MEN2B features medullary thyroid carcinoma, pheochromocytoma, mucosal neuromas, and marfanoid habitus, and characteristically spares the parathyroid glands.

options.text: Familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia; inactivating mutation of the calcium-sensing receptor
options.explanation: This causes lifelong mild hypercalcemia with an only mildly elevated PTH, a low urinary calcium-to-creatinine clearance ratio, and no stones or associated tumors. A PTH of 760 pg/mL is far too high.

questions.takeaway: MEN1 = the three P's (parathyroid, pancreas, pituitary), autosomal dominant loss of the menin tumor suppressor; hyperparathyroidism is usually the earliest sign.

questions.objective: Sequence management when medullary thyroid carcinoma and pheochromocytoma coexist
questions.stem: A 47-year-old man with a history of primary hyperparathyroidism presents with an anterior neck mass. Serum calcitonin is markedly elevated and biopsy shows nests of tumor cells in an amyloid-rich stroma. Several relatives have had "thyroid problems." Total thyroidectomy is planned. Which is the most important step before that operation?

options.text: Screen for pheochromocytoma with plasma free metanephrines and treat it first if present
options.explanation: Correct. Medullary thyroid carcinoma plus hyperparathyroidism plus a family history indicates MEN2A, caused by germline gain-of-function RET mutations. Roughly half of these patients harbor a pheochromocytoma, and anesthesia or surgical manipulation in an unprepared patient can precipitate a lethal catecholamine crisis. The pheochromocytoma is therefore always excluded — and resected first, after α-blockade — before any other operation.

options.text: Examine the lips and tongue for mucosal neuromas and assess for marfanoid habitus
options.explanation: These are MEN2B features, and MEN2B characteristically does not include hyperparathyroidism. Even if present, they would not change the immediate perioperative priority.

options.text: Measure fasting insulin and C-peptide to exclude an insulinoma
options.explanation: Pancreatic islet tumors are a MEN1 manifestation and are not part of MEN2.

options.text: Send the biopsy for BRAF V600E testing
options.explanation: BRAF mutations characterize papillary thyroid carcinoma. Amyloid stroma and elevated calcitonin identify a medullary (parafollicular C-cell) tumor.

options.text: Obtain a pituitary MRI to exclude a prolactinoma
options.explanation: Pituitary adenomas belong to MEN1. Medullary thyroid carcinoma places this patient in the MEN2 group instead.

questions.takeaway: In any MEN2 patient, exclude and treat pheochromocytoma before any other surgery — unprepared anesthesia can trigger a fatal catecholamine crisis.

questions.objective: Differentiate MEN2A from MEN2B
questions.stem: A 12-year-old boy has a marfanoid habitus, everted eyelids, nodular bumps on the lips and tongue, and long-standing constipation attributed to intestinal ganglioneuromatosis. Serum calcitonin is elevated. Which finding would be LEAST expected in this syndrome?

options.explanation: MEN2B is caused by germline activating RET mutations, most often M918T, which correlates with the aggressive phenotype.

Correct. Mucosal neuromas, marfanoid habitus, and intestinal ganglioneuromatosis identify MEN2B, and parathyroid disease is characteristically absent — that is the single feature separating MEN2B from MEN2A. MEN2B also carries the earliest and most aggressive medullary thyroid carcinoma, which is why prophylactic thyroidectomy is done in infancy or early childhood.
Medullary thyroid carcinoma occurs in essentially all patients with MEN2B and is the reason the calcitonin is elevated.
Pheochromocytoma occurs in roughly half of MEN2B patients, as in MEN2A, and must be excluded before any surgery.
All MEN2 subtypes are autosomal dominant, although a substantial fraction of MEN2B cases arise de novo.

questions.takeaway: MEN2A = medullary thyroid carcinoma + pheochromocytoma + hyperparathyroidism. MEN2B = medullary thyroid carcinoma + pheochromocytoma + mucosal neuromas and marfanoid habitus, with NO parathyroid disease.

questions.objective: Distinguish adrenocortical carcinoma from a benign functioning adenoma
questions.stem: A 46-year-old woman describes three months of rapidly progressive facial hair growth, deepening of her voice, and temporal hair loss, together with new hypertension and easy bruising. DHEA-sulfate and 24-hour urinary free cortisol are both markedly elevated. Imaging shows a 12-cm left adrenal mass invading the perinephric fat, with enlarged periaortic nodes. Which is the most likely diagnosis?

options.explanation: A chromaffin tumor causes paroxysmal headache, palpitations, and diaphoresis with elevated metanephrines. It does not secrete cortisol or androgens.
By definition an incidentaloma is hormonally silent and found unintentionally. This mass is clearly hypersecreting two steroid classes.
These are usually under 2 cm and present with hypertension and hypokalemia, not virilization or hypercortisolism.

Correct. Adrenocortical carcinomas are typically functional and often announce themselves with virilization, and they are large and invasive with atrophic adjacent cortex and early spread to regional and periaortic nodes, then hematogenously to lung. Co-secretion of more than one steroid class — glucocorticoid plus androgen here — over a span of months reinforces the diagnosis. Some cases are syndromic (Li-Fraumeni, Beckwith-Wiedemann).

Adenomas are well-circumscribed and usually no more than about 2.5 cm, with adjacent cortex of normal thickness, and roughly 60% are non-functional. When one does secrete, it secretes a single steroid class. Neither the size, the invasion, the nodal spread, nor the virilization fits an adenoma.

questions.takeaway: Large size, rapid onset, and mixed glucocorticoid-plus-androgen excess point to adrenocortical carcinoma rather than a benign functioning adenoma.

questions.objective: Anticipate the complications of long-term pharmacologic glucocorticoid exposure
questions.stem: A 34-year-old man with ulcerative colitis is hospitalized with an acute flare and started on prednisone 60 mg daily with a planned taper. He asks what would happen if he ended up needing the drug long term. Which complication is he most likely to develop?

options.explanation: Correct. Glucocorticoids are the leading cause of drug-induced osteoporosis. They suppress osteoblast function and promote osteocyte apoptosis, increase RANKL-driven bone resorption, reduce intestinal calcium absorption, and induce hypogonadism. Bone loss is fastest in the first six to twelve months, so calcium and vitamin D supplementation, weight-bearing exercise, and consideration of a bisphosphonate begin early.
Spider angiomata reflect the altered estrogen handling of chronic liver disease. Glucocorticoids cause skin thinning, purpura, and striae instead.

The opposite occurs. Exogenous glucocorticoid suppresses ACTH, causing adrenal atrophy — which is why abrupt withdrawal can precipitate secondary adrenal insufficiency and why prolonged courses must be tapered.
Agranulocytosis is characteristic of thionamides, clozapine, and some other agents. Glucocorticoids actually raise the neutrophil count by demargination and delayed apoptosis.
This follows restoration of immune function, typically after starting antiretroviral therapy. Glucocorticoids suppress immunity and are in fact sometimes used to treat it.

questions.takeaway: Long-term glucocorticoids cause iatrogenic Cushing syndrome, rapid early bone loss with fragility fracture, and HPA suppression — supplement calcium and vitamin D and never stop abruptly.
