questions.topic: Approach to atypical genitalia in the newborn
questions.objective: Explain why a DSD is a medical emergency in the newborn period
questions.stem: A term newborn has a 1.5-cm phallic structure, a single perineal opening, partially fused labioscrotal folds, and no palpable gonads. The parents ask whether anything needs to be done urgently. Which concern most justifies urgent evaluation?

options.text: Salt-wasting congenital adrenal hyperplasia, which can cause fatal adrenal crisis within the first two weeks of life
options.explanation: Correct. CAH is both the most common cause of atypical genitalia in a 46,XX newborn and the only cause that is immediately life-threatening. Cortisol and aldosterone deficiency produce vomiting, hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, hypoglycemia, and hypovolemic shock, typically in the first one to three weeks — after discharge. Electrolytes, glucose, and 17α-hydroxyprogesterone are therefore checked promptly, and stress-dose glucocorticoid is given if crisis is suspected.

options.text: Sex of rearing must be assigned within the first 24 hours to avoid psychological harm
options.explanation: This is the opposite of current practice. Assignment is deliberately deferred until karyotype, hormonal, and anatomic data are available and a multidisciplinary team has counseled the family. Rushing the decision is itself a recognized harm.
Isolated hypospadias with descended testes is not a DSD and is managed electively. Hypospadias accompanied by non-palpable gonads, as here, is precisely what mandates evaluation.
Complete androgen insensitivity produces unambiguously female-appearing external genitalia, so it is not usually detected in the newborn period, and it carries no acute metabolic risk.

Turner syndrome presents with female external genitalia, sometimes with lymphedema or a webbed neck, and its cardiac and renal anomalies warrant evaluation — but it does not cause atypical genitalia or adrenal crisis.

questions.takeaway: Atypical genitalia in a newborn is an emergency because of one diagnosis: salt-wasting CAH. Check electrolytes, glucose, and 17α-hydroxyprogesterone before the baby goes home.

questions.topic: Approach to atypical genitalia in the newborn
questions.objective: Recognize the initial evaluation of a newborn with atypical genitalia
questions.stem: A newborn is noted at delivery to have atypical genitalia with non-palpable gonads. A multidisciplinary team is assembled. Which set of initial investigations is most appropriate?

options.text: MRI of the brain to evaluate the hypothalamic-pituitary axis
options.explanation: Central causes of hypogonadism such as Kallmann syndrome are considered when puberty fails, not in a newborn with atypical genitalia.

options.text: Defer all testing until six months of age to allow the family time to adjust
options.explanation: Deferring is unsafe: a salt-wasting crisis typically occurs within the first two to three weeks. Prompt evaluation and unhurried decisions about sex of rearing are compatible, not in conflict.

options.text: Immediate gonadal biopsy to establish gonadal histology
options.explanation: Gonadal biopsy is invasive and is reserved for selected cases, such as suspected ovotesticular DSD or gonadal dysgenesis with tumor risk, after non-invasive testing has narrowed the differential.

options.text: Karyotype with FISH for SRY, serum 17α-hydroxyprogesterone, serum electrolytes and glucose, and pelvic and inguinal ultrasound
options.explanation: Correct. These four answer the questions that drive every subsequent decision: what are the sex chromosomes, is this CAH, is the infant in metabolic danger, and what internal structures (uterus, gonads) are present. Testosterone, dihydrotestosterone, AMH, LH, and FSH are added according to the karyotype result.

options.text: A trial of intramuscular testosterone to assess phallic growth
options.explanation: An hCG or testosterone stimulation test has a role in evaluating 46,XY DSD later in the workup, but it is not an initial study and does not address the urgent question of adrenal insufficiency.

questions.takeaway: First four studies in a newborn with atypical genitalia: karyotype/SRY, 17α-hydroxyprogesterone, electrolytes and glucose, and pelvic ultrasound.

questions.objective: Differentiate 46,XY DSDs by pubertal breast development, blood pressure, and Müllerian structures
questions.stem: A 16-year-old raised as a girl is evaluated for primary amenorrhea. There is no breast development and no pubic or axillary hair. Blood pressure is 158/98 mm Hg and potassium is 2.9 mEq/L. Karyotype is 46,XY. Ultrasound shows no uterus and intra-abdominal gonads. Which diagnosis best explains all of these findings?

options.explanation: Correct. Loss of CYP17A1 blocks testosterone synthesis, so a 46,XY fetus does not virilize and the external genitalia appear female. Sertoli cells still make AMH, so the Müllerian ducts regress and there is no uterus. Because both gonadal and adrenal sex steroids are absent, puberty brings neither breasts nor pubic hair. Meanwhile ACTH drives accumulation of 11-deoxycorticosterone and corticosterone, whose mineralocorticoid activity gives hypertension with hypokalemia — the finding that no other option on this list explains.
MRKH occurs in 46,XX individuals with functioning ovaries, so breast development and pubic hair are normal and only the uterus and upper vagina are absent. The karyotype here is 46,XY.

Streak gonads make neither testosterone nor AMH, so the Müllerian ducts persist and a uterus IS present — which is inconsistent with this ultrasound. Patients are also normotensive with hypergonadotropic hypogonadism.
Testosterone is normal, so patients virilize substantially at puberty with deepening voice and muscle development, and blood pressure and potassium are normal.

CAIS shares the female external phenotype, the absent uterus (AMH still regresses the Müllerian ducts), the intra-abdominal testes, and the sparse pubic and axillary hair. But androgen biosynthesis is normal in CAIS — serum testosterone sits in the male reference range, because the defect is in the androgen receptor — whereas here testosterone synthesis itself is blocked. CAIS also causes neither hypertension nor hypokalemia, and the available testosterone is aromatized peripherally, so breast development at puberty is normal rather than absent.

questions.takeaway: In 46,XY DSD, absent breast development plus hypertension and hypokalemia separates 17α-hydroxylase deficiency from CAIS; a present uterus points instead to gonadal dysgenesis.

questions.topic: Congenital adrenal hyperplasia and newborn screening
questions.objective: Explain the role of newborn screening in the diagnosis of congenital adrenal hyperplasia
questions.stem: Newborn screening for congenital adrenal hyperplasia measures 17α-hydroxyprogesterone on the dried blood spot. Why are affected male infants more dependent on this screen than affected female infants for timely diagnosis?

options.text: 21-hydroxylase deficiency is X-linked, so males are affected more severely
options.explanation: CYP21A2 is on chromosome 6 and the disorder is autosomal recessive. Males and females are affected with equal frequency and equal biochemical severity.

options.text: Male infants have physiologically higher 17α-hydroxyprogesterone levels, making the test more sensitive in boys
options.explanation: Sex does not meaningfully change the assay's performance. Gestational-age-adjusted cutoffs matter far more, since preterm infants have higher baseline levels and generate false positives.

options.text: Male infants have a more severe enzyme deficiency on average
options.explanation: The severity of the genotype is independent of sex; what differs is only how visible the androgen excess is at birth.

options.text: Affected 46,XY infants have normal-appearing external genitalia at birth, so without screening the diagnosis is not suspected until a salt-wasting crisis occurs
options.explanation: Correct. Excess adrenal androgen has no visible effect on a male fetus whose genitalia are already virilized by testicular testosterone, so nothing prompts evaluation. An affected 46,XX infant, by contrast, is often identified at birth from clitoromegaly and labial fusion. Males therefore reach a crisis — typically at one to three weeks with vomiting, hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, and shock — unless the screen catches them, which is the principal reason CAH is on the newborn panel.

options.text: Placental aromatase protects female fetuses from developing the enzyme deficiency
options.explanation: Placental aromatase does shield the fetus from maternal androgens, but it does not prevent the deficiency and does not prevent virilization by the fetus's own adrenal androgens — which is exactly why affected 46,XX infants are virilized.

questions.takeaway: Newborn screening for CAH exists chiefly to catch affected boys, whose genitalia look normal and who would otherwise present in salt-wasting crisis after discharge.
